explanatories.ContinuousLinearMap.snd: The second projection map from a product of two modules to the second module is a continuous linear map.

explanatories.ContDiffAt.log: The logarithm of a continuously differentiable function at a point is also continuously differentiable at that point, provided the function's value at that point is non-zero.

MeasureTheory.lintegral_rpow_eq_lintegra.code:
MeasureTheory.lintegral_rpow_eq_lintegral_meas_le_mul.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [MeasurableSpace α] {f : α → ℝ}
  (μ : Measure α) (f_nn : 0 ≤ᶠ[ae μ] f) (f_mble : AEMeasurable f μ) {p : ℝ} (p_pos : 0 < p) :
  ∫⁻ (ω : α), ENNReal.ofReal (f ω ^ p) ∂μ =
    ENNReal.ofReal p * ∫⁻ (t : ℝ) in Ioi 0, μ {a | t ≤ f a} * ENNReal.ofReal (t ^ (p - 1))
MeasureTheory.lintegral_rpow_eq_lintegra.comment:
An application of the layer cake formula / Cavalieri's principle / tail probability formula:

For a nonnegative function `f` on a measure space, the Lebesgue integral of `f` can
be written (roughly speaking) as: `∫⁻ f^p ∂μ = p * ∫⁻ t in 0..∞, t^(p-1) * μ {ω | f(ω) ≥ t}`.

See `MeasureTheory.lintegral_rpow_eq_lintegral_meas_lt_mul` for a version with sets of the form
`{ω | f(ω) > t}` instead.

explanatories.MeasureTheory.ae: The "almost everywhere" filter represents the collection of sets that differ from a given set by at most a collection of co-null sets.
explanatories.AEMeasurable: This definition characterizes a function as almost everywhere measurable if it agrees with some measurable function on all but a negligible subset of its domain.
explanatories.ENNReal.ofReal: This definition describes a function that converts a real number into the extended nonnegative real numbers, returning the number itself if it is nonnegative and zero if it is negative.
explanatories.Set.Ioi: This definition denotes the set of elements that are strictly greater than a specified element in a preorder structure, resulting in a left-open and right-infinite interval.

MeasureTheory.lintegral_rpow_eq_lintegra.description: The theorem conveys that the Lebesgue integral of a nonnegative function raised to a positive power can be expressed as a product of that power and another integral involving the measure of the set where the function exceeds certain thresholds.

  [NormedRing 𝔸] [NormedAlgebra 𝕂 𝔸] [CompleteSpace 𝔸] (h : 0 < (expSeries 𝕂 𝔸).radius) : HasStrictFDerivAt (exp 𝕂) 1 0
hasStrictFDerivAt_exp_zero_of_radius_pos.comment:
The exponential in a Banach algebra `𝔸` over a normed field `𝕂` has strict Fréchet derivative

Real.sqPartialHomeomorph.comment:
Local homeomorph between `(0, +∞)` and `(0, +∞)` with `toFun = (· ^ 2)` and
`invFun = Real.sqrt`.

explanatories.Real.sqrt: The square root function is defined for real numbers, returning zero for negative inputs.
explanatories.Set.Ioi: This definition denotes the set of elements that are strictly greater than a specified element in a preorder structure, resulting in a left-open and right-infinite interval.
explanatories.Set.mem_Ioi: This theorem asserts that an element is part of the interval consisting of elements strictly greater than a given element in a preorder structure if and only if it is greater than that element.
explanatories.pow_pos: In a strict ordered semiring, if a positive element is raised to a natural number power, the result remains positive.
explanatories.Real.sqrt_pos: The square root of a positive real number is positive if and only if the original number is also positive.
explanatories.Real.sqrt_sq: The square root of the square of any nonnegative real number equals that original nonnegative number.
explanatories.le_of_lt: This theorem asserts that if one element is strictly less than another in a preorder, then it is also less than or equal to that element.
explanatories.Real.sq_sqrt: The square of the square root of a nonnegative real number is equal to the original number itself.
explanatories.isOpen_Ioi: This theorem states that the interval of all points greater than a given point in a linear ordered topological space with a closed lower interval topology is an open set.
explanatories.continuous_pow: The function that raises elements to a natural number power is continuous in a topological space where multiplication is continuous.
explanatories.Continuous.continuousOn: If a function is continuous on its entire domain, it is also continuous on any subset of that domain.
explanatories.continuousOn_id: The identity function is continuous on any given set within a topological space.
explanatories.ContinuousOn.sqrt: The square root of a continuous function defined on a set remains continuous on that set.

Real.sqPartialHomeomorph.fullDefinition: noncomputable def sqPartialHomeomorph : PartialHomeomorph ℝ ℝ where   toFun x := x ^ 2   invFun := (√·)   source := Ioi 0   target := Ioi 0   map_source' _ h := mem_Ioi.2 (pow_pos (mem_Ioi.1 h) _)   map_target' _ h := mem_Ioi.2 (sqrt_pos.2 h)   left_inv' _ h := sqrt_sq (le_of_lt h)   right_inv' _ h := sq_sqrt (le_of_lt h)   open_source := isOpen_Ioi   open_target := isOpen_Ioi   continuousOn_toFun := (continuous_pow 2).continuousOn   continuousOn_invFun := continuousOn_id.sqrt
Real.sqPartialHomeomorph.description: There exists a local homeomorphism between the positive real numbers that maps each number to its square and its inverse maps each number back to its square root.

expNegInvGlue.comment:
`expNegInvGlue` is the real function given by `x ↦ exp (-1/x)` for `x > 0` and `0`
for `x ≤ 0`. It is a basic building block to construct smooth partitions of unity. Its main property
is that it vanishes for `x ≤ 0`, it is positive for `x > 0`, and the junction between the two
behaviors is flat enough to retain smoothness. The fact that this function is `C^∞` is proved in
`expNegInvGlue.contDiff`.

Complex.Gammaℝ.comment:
Deligne's archimedean Gamma factor for a real infinite place.

See "Valeurs de fonctions L et periodes d'integrales" § 5.3. Note that this is not the same as
`Real.Gamma`; in particular it is a function `ℂ → ℂ`.
Complex.Gammaℝ.fullDefinition: noncomputable def Gammaℝ (s : ℂ) := π ^ (-s / 2) * Gamma (s / 2)
Complex.Gammaℝ.description: This definition describes a complex-valued function that serves as Deligne's archimedean Gamma factor at a real infinite place, distinct from the real Gamma function.

Complex.Gammaℂ.comment:
Deligne's archimedean Gamma factor for a complex infinite place.

See "Valeurs de fonctions L et periodes d'integrales" § 5.3. (Some authors omit the factor of 2).
Note that this is not the same as `Complex.Gamma`.
Complex.Gammaℂ.fullDefinition: noncomputable def Gammaℂ (s : ℂ) := 2 * (2 * π) ^ (-s) * Gamma s
Complex.Gammaℂ.description: This definition describes a complex-valued function that represents Deligne's archimedean Gamma factor at a complex infinite place, differing from the standard complex Gamma function.

Complex.Gammaℝ_def.description: This theorem establishes that the complex-valued function representing Deligne's archimedean Gamma factor at a real infinite place is equivalent to a specific expression involving π and the standard Gamma function.

Complex.Gammaℂ_def.description: This theorem asserts that the complex-valued function representing Deligne's archimedean Gamma factor at a complex infinite place equals a specific expression involving π and the standard Gamma function.

explanatories.Ne.eq_1: This theorem states that the inequality of two elements is equivalent to the negation of their equality.

Complex.Gammaℝ.eq_1.description: This theorem states that the complex-valued function representing Deligne's archimedean Gamma factor at a real infinite place is equal to a specific expression involving π and the standard Gamma function.

Complex.Gammaℝ_eq_zero_iff.description: This theorem states that the complex-valued function representing Deligne's archimedean Gamma factor at a real infinite place is zero if and only if the argument is a negative even integer.

Complex.Gammaℝ_one_sub_mul_Gammaℝ_one_ad.comment: Reformulation of the reflection formula in terms of `Gammaℝ`.
Complex.Gammaℝ_one_sub_mul_Gammaℝ_one_ad.description: This theorem reformulates the reflection formula for the real Gamma function, stating that the product of the Gamma function evaluated at one minus and one plus a complex argument equals the reciprocal of the cosine function evaluated at half the argument multiplied by π.

Complex.Gammaℝ_mul_Gammaℝ_add_one.comment: Reformulation of the doubling formula in terms of `Gammaℝ`.

explanatories.Complex.Gammaℂ: This definition describes a complex-valued function that represents Deligne's archimedean Gamma factor at a complex infinite place, differing from the standard complex Gamma function.

Complex.Gammaℝ_mul_Gammaℝ_add_one.description: This theorem reformulates the doubling property of the Gamma function to express the product of Deligne's archimedean Gamma factor at a real infinite place and its increment by one as equivalent to the corresponding complex-valued Gamma factor.

Complex.Gammaℝ_one.description: This theorem states that the value of Deligne's archimedean Gamma factor at one for a real infinite place is equal to one.

Complex.Gammaℂ_one.description: This theorem establishes that the value of Deligne's archimedean Gamma factor at one is equal to the reciprocal of π.

Formulation of reflection formula tailored to functional equations of L-functions of even

Complex.Gammaℂ_add_one.description: This theorem states that for a non-zero complex number, the value of the complex Gamma function at one plus that number is equal to the product of the Gamma function at that number and a specific fraction involving that number and π.

A property ensuring that the tangent cone to `s` at any of its points spans a dense subset of
the whole space. The main role of this property is to ensure that the differential along `s` is
unique, hence this name. The uniqueness it asserts is proved in `UniqueDiffOn.eq` in
`Fderiv.Basic`.

HasFDerivWithinAt.code:
HasFDerivWithinAt.{u_1, u_2, u_3} {𝕜 : Type u_1} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {E : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup E]
  [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] {F : Type u_3} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] (f : E → F) (f' : E →L[𝕜] F) (s : Set E)
  (x : E) : Prop
HasFDerivWithinAt.comment:
A function `f` has the continuous linear map `f'` as derivative at `x` within a set `s` if
`f x' = f x + f' (x' - x) + o (x' - x)` when `x'` tends to `x` inside `s`.

explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.

HasFDerivWithinAt.fullDefinition: def HasFDerivWithinAt (f : E → F) (f' : E →L[𝕜] F) (s : Set E) (x : E) :=   HasFDerivAtFilter f f' x (𝓝[s] x)
HasFDerivWithinAt.description: A function has a specified continuous linear derivative at a point within a set if its behavior around that point can be approximated by the linear map in the limit as the input approaches the point from within the set.

HasStrictFDerivAt.code:
HasStrictFDerivAt.{u_1, u_2, u_3} {𝕜 : Type u_1} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {E : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup E]
  [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] {F : Type u_3} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] (f : E → F) (f' : E →L[𝕜] F) (x : E) : Prop
HasStrictFDerivAt.comment:
A function `f` has derivative `f'` at `a` in the sense of *strict differentiability*
if `f x - f y - f' (x - y) = o(x - y)` as `x, y → a`. This form of differentiability is required,
e.g., by the inverse function theorem. Any `C^1` function on a vector space over `ℝ` is strictly
differentiable but this definition works, e.g., for vector spaces over `p`-adic numbers.
HasStrictFDerivAt.fullDefinition: def HasStrictFDerivAt (f : E → F) (f' : E →L[𝕜] F) (x : E) :=   (fun p : E × E => f p.1 - f p.2 - f' (p.1 - p.2)) =o[𝓝 (x, x)] fun p : E × E => p.1 - p.2
HasStrictFDerivAt.description: A function has a specified continuous linear derivative at a point in the sense of strict differentiability if the difference between the function values around that point can be approximated by the linear map as the inputs approach the point.

e.g., by the inverse function theorem. Any `C^1` function on a vector space over `ℝ` is strictly

HasFDerivWithinAt.lim.comment:
If a function f has a derivative f' at x, a rescaled version of f around x converges to f',
i.e., `n (f (x + (1/n) v) - f x)` converges to `f' v`. More generally, if `c n` tends to infinity
and `c n * d n` tends to `v`, then `c n * (f (x + d n) - f x)` tends to `f' v`. This lemma expresses
this fact, for functions having a derivative within a set. Its specific formulation is useful for
tangent cone related discussions.

norm_fderiv_le_of_lip'.code:
norm_fderiv_le_of_lip'.{u_1, u_2, u_3} (𝕜 : Type u_1) [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {E : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup E]
  [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] {F : Type u_3} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] {f : E → F} {x₀ : E} {C : ℝ} (hC₀ : 0 ≤ C)
  (hlip : ∀ᶠ (x : E) in 𝓝 x₀, ‖f x - f x₀‖ ≤ C * ‖x - x₀‖) : ‖fderiv 𝕜 f x₀‖ ≤ C
norm_fderiv_le_of_lip'.comment:
Converse to the mean value inequality: if `f` is `C`-lipschitz
on a neighborhood of `x₀` then its derivative at `x₀` has norm bounded by `C`. This version
only assumes that `‖f x - f x₀‖ ≤ C * ‖x - x₀‖` in a neighborhood of `x`.

explanatories.HasStrictFDerivAt.comp: If two functions possess strict derivatives at a point and if the first function maps to the second function's domain, then their composition also has a strict derivative at that point with the appropriately derived composition, demonstrating a version of the chain rule for strict differentiability.
explanatories.ContinuousLinearEquiv.comp_fderiv: The derivative of the composition of a continuous linear equivalence with a function at a given point equals the composition of the linear equivalence and the derivative of the function at that point.
explanatories.DifferentiableWithinAt.comp: If a function is differentiable within a specific set at a point and another function is differentiable at the image of that point under the first function while appropriately mapping sets, then the composition of the two functions is also differentiable within the original set at that point.
explanatories.HasFDerivWithinAt.comp: If a function has a derivative at a point within a specific set and another function has a derivative at the image of that point under the first function within an appropriately mapped set, then the composition of the two functions also has a derivative within the original set at that point.
explanatories.LinearIsometryEquiv.fderiv: The derivative of a linear isometry equivalence at a point equals the linear map associated with its underlying linear equivalence.

linear_isometry_equiv.comp_fderiv.description: The derivative of the composition of a function with a linear isometry equivalence at a point is equal to the composition of the linear equivalence with the derivative of the original function at that point.

HasStrictFDerivAt.of_local_left_inverse.comment:
If `f (g y) = y` for `y` in some neighborhood of `a`, `g` is continuous at `a`, and `f` has an
invertible derivative `f'` at `g a` in the strict sense, then `g` has the derivative `f'⁻¹` at `a`
in the strict sense.

This is one of the easy parts of the inverse function theorem: it assumes that we already have an
inverse function.

PartialHomeomorph.hasStrictFDerivAt_symm.comment:
If `f` is a partial homeomorphism defined on a neighbourhood of `f.symm a`, and `f` has an
invertible derivative `f'` in the sense of strict differentiability at `f.symm a`, then `f.symm` has
the derivative `f'⁻¹` at `a`.

This is one of the easy parts of the inverse function theorem: it assumes that we already have
an inverse function.

  [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] {G : Type u_4} [NormedAddCommGroup G] [NormedSpace 𝕜 G] {x : E} {H : Type u_6}

explanatories.FormalMultilinearSeries: A formal multilinear series is defined as a collection of multilinear maps that relate vectors from a source space to a target space over a specified ring.
explanatories.HasFDerivAt: A function has a specified continuous linear derivative at a point if its behavior around that point can be approximated by the linear map in the limit as the input approaches the point.
explanatories.HasStrictFDerivAt.hasFDerivAt: If a function has a strictly defined derivative at a point, then it also has a general derivative at that point.
explanatories.HasFPowerSeriesAt.hasFDerivAt: If a function has a power series representation at a point, it also possesses a derivative at that point which corresponds to the first derivative term of the power series.
explanatories.FormalMultilinearSeries.changeOrigin: Changing the origin of a formal multilinear series allows it to represent the same series evaluated at a translated point in the source space.
explanatories.HasFPowerSeriesOnBall.changeOrigin: If a function has a power series expansion on a ball of a certain radius, it can also be represented by a modified power series centered at a shifted point within that ball, with a corresponding reduced radius.
explanatories.HasFiniteFPowerSeriesOnBall.changeOrigin: If a function has a finite power series expansion around a point within a certain radius, then shifting the center of that expansion results in another finite power series around the new center with a reduced radius.
explanatories.ContinuousLinearMap.hasFDerivAt: A continuous linear map has a derivative at a point if it can be locally approximated by the linear map as inputs approach that point.

HasFPowerSeriesOnBall.hasFDerivAt.description: If a function has a power series representation within a radius around a point, it has a derivative at any point within that radius, which is determined by the first derivative term of the power series adjusted for that point.

explanatories.FormalMultilinearSeries: A formal multilinear series is defined as a collection of multilinear maps that relate vectors from a source space to a target space over a specified ring.
explanatories.HasFDerivAt: A function has a specified continuous linear derivative at a point if its behavior around that point can be approximated by the linear map in the limit as the input approaches the point.
explanatories.HasStrictFDerivAt.hasFDerivAt: If a function has a strictly defined derivative at a point, then it also has a general derivative at that point.
explanatories.HasFPowerSeriesAt.hasFDerivAt: If a function has a power series representation at a point, it also possesses a derivative at that point which corresponds to the first derivative term of the power series.
explanatories.FormalMultilinearSeries.changeOrigin: Changing the origin of a formal multilinear series allows it to represent the same series evaluated at a translated point in the source space.
explanatories.HasFPowerSeriesOnBall.changeOrigin: If a function has a power series expansion on a ball of a certain radius, it can also be represented by a modified power series centered at a shifted point within that ball, with a corresponding reduced radius.
explanatories.HasFPowerSeriesOnBall.hasFDerivAt: If a function has a power series representation within a radius around a point, it has a derivative at any point within that radius, which is determined by the first derivative term of the power series adjusted for that point.
explanatories.HasFiniteFPowerSeriesOnBall.changeOrigin: If a function has a finite power series expansion around a point within a certain radius, then shifting the center of that expansion results in another finite power series around the new center with a reduced radius.
explanatories.ContinuousLinearMap.hasFDerivAt: A continuous linear map has a derivative at a point if it can be locally approximated by the linear map as inputs approach that point.

HasFiniteFPowerSeriesOnBall.hasFDerivAt.description: If a function has a finite power series expansion around a point within a specified radius, then it has a derivative at nearby points given by a modified version of the original series.

Convex.taylor_approx_two_segment.{u_1, u_2} {E : Type u_1} {F : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
  [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F] {s : Set E} (s_conv : Convex ℝ s) {f : E → F} {f' : E → E →L[ℝ] F}
  {f'' : E →L[ℝ] E →L[ℝ] F} (hf : ∀ x ∈ interior s, HasFDerivAt f (f' x) x) {x : E} (xs : x ∈ s)
  (hx : HasFDerivWithinAt f' f'' (interior s) x) {v w : E} (hv : x + v ∈ interior s) (hw : x + v + w ∈ interior s) :
  (fun h =>
      f (x + h • v + h • w) - f (x + h • v) - h • (f' x) w - h ^ 2 • (f'' v) w - (h ^ 2 / 2) • (f'' w) w) =o[𝓝[>] 0]
    fun h => h ^ 2
Convex.taylor_approx_two_segment.comment:
Assume that `f` is differentiable inside a convex set `s`, and that its derivative `f'` is
differentiable at a point `x`. Then, given two vectors `v` and `w` pointing inside `s`, one can
Taylor-expand to order two the function `f` on the segment `[x + h v, x + h (v + w)]`, giving a
bilinear estimate for `f (x + hv + hw) - f (x + hv)` in terms of `f' w` and of `f'' ⬝ w`, up to
`o(h^2)`.

Convex.isLittleO_alternate_sum_square.{u_1, u_2} {E : Type u_1} {F : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
  [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F] {s : Set E} (s_conv : Convex ℝ s) {f : E → F} {f' : E → E →L[ℝ] F}
  {f'' : E →L[ℝ] E →L[ℝ] F} (hf : ∀ x ∈ interior s, HasFDerivAt f (f' x) x) {x : E} (xs : x ∈ s)
  (hx : HasFDerivWithinAt f' f'' (interior s) x) {v w : E} (h4v : x + 4 • v ∈ interior s)
  (h4w : x + 4 • w ∈ interior s) :
  (fun h =>
      f (x + h • (2 • v + 2 • w)) + f (x + h • (v + w)) - f (x + h • (2 • v + w)) - f (x + h • (v + 2 • w)) -
        h ^ 2 • (f'' v) w) =o[𝓝[>] 0]
    fun h => h ^ 2
Convex.isLittleO_alternate_sum_square.comment:
One can get `f'' v w` as the limit of `h ^ (-2)` times the alternate sum of the values of `f`
along the vertices of a quadrilateral with sides `h v` and `h w` based at `x`.
In a setting where `f` is not guaranteed to be continuous at `f`, we can still

convex.is_o_alternate_sum_square.code:
Convex.isLittleO_alternate_sum_square.{u_1, u_2} {E : Type u_1} {F : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
  [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F] {s : Set E} (s_conv : Convex ℝ s) {f : E → F} {f' : E → E →L[ℝ] F}
  {f'' : E →L[ℝ] E →L[ℝ] F} (hf : ∀ x ∈ interior s, HasFDerivAt f (f' x) x) {x : E} (xs : x ∈ s)
  (hx : HasFDerivWithinAt f' f'' (interior s) x) {v w : E} (h4v : x + 4 • v ∈ interior s)
  (h4w : x + 4 • w ∈ interior s) :
  (fun h =>
      f (x + h • (2 • v + 2 • w)) + f (x + h • (v + w)) - f (x + h • (2 • v + w)) - f (x + h • (v + 2 • w)) -
        h ^ 2 • (f'' v) w) =o[𝓝[>] 0]
    fun h => h ^ 2
convex.is_o_alternate_sum_square.comment:
One can get `f'' v w` as the limit of `h ^ (-2)` times the alternate sum of the values of `f`
along the vertices of a quadrilateral with sides `h v` and `h w` based at `x`.
In a setting where `f` is not guaranteed to be continuous at `f`, we can still
get this if we use a quadrilateral based at `h v + h w`.

  [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] {F : Type u_3} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] (f : E → F) (L : E →L[𝕜] F) (r ε : ℝ) :
  Set E
FDerivMeasurableAux.A.comment:
The set `A f L r ε` is the set of points `x` around which the function `f` is well approximated
at scale `r` by the linear map `L`, up to an error `ε`. We tweak the definition to make sure that
this is an open set.

explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.
explanatories.Set.Ioc: This definition denotes the set of elements that are strictly greater than one given element and less than or equal to another in a preorder structure, forming a left-open and right-closed interval.
explanatories.Metric.ball: The set defined includes all points within a specified distance from a given point in a pseudo-metric space.

FDerivMeasurableAux.A.fullDefinition: def A (f : E → F) (L : E →L[𝕜] F) (r ε : ℝ) : Set E :=   { x | ∃ r' ∈ Ioc (r / 2) r, ∀ y ∈ ball x r', ∀ z ∈ ball x r', ‖f z - f y - L (z - y)‖ < ε * r }
FDerivMeasurableAux.A.description: The set described consists of points in the domain where a function is closely approximated by a linear map within a specified accuracy margin.

RightDerivMeasurableAux.A.code:
RightDerivMeasurableAux.A.{u_1} {F : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F] (f : ℝ → F) (L : F) (r ε : ℝ) :
  Set ℝ
RightDerivMeasurableAux.A.comment:
The set `A f L r ε` is the set of points `x` around which the function `f` is well approximated
at scale `r` by the linear map `h ↦ h • L`, up to an error `ε`. We tweak the definition to
make sure that this is open on the right.

explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.
explanatories.Set.Ioc: This definition denotes the set of elements that are strictly greater than one given element and less than or equal to another in a preorder structure, forming a left-open and right-closed interval.
explanatories.FDerivMeasurableAux.A: The set described consists of points in the domain where a function is closely approximated by a linear map within a specified accuracy margin.
explanatories.Set.Icc: This definition describes the set of elements that are greater than or equal to one given element and less than or equal to another in a preorder structure, forming a left-closed and right-closed interval.

RightDerivMeasurableAux.A.fullDefinition: def A (f : ℝ → F) (L : F) (r ε : ℝ) : Set ℝ :=   { x | ∃ r' ∈ Ioc (r / 2) r, ∀ᵉ (y ∈ Icc x (x + r')) (z ∈ Icc x (x + r')),     ‖f z - f y - (z - y) • L‖ ≤ ε * r }
RightDerivMeasurableAux.A.description: The set defined captures the points where a function is well approximated by a linear map up to a specified error, ensuring that this set is open to the right.

  (r s ε : ℝ) : Set ℝ
RightDerivMeasurableAux.B.comment:
The set `B f K r s ε` is the set of points `x` around which there exists a vector
`L` belonging to `K` (a given set of vectors) such that `h • L` approximates well `f (x + h)`
(up to an error `ε`), simultaneously at scales `r` and `s`.

explanatories.RightDerivMeasurableAux.A: The set defined captures the points where a function is well approximated by a linear map up to a specified error, ensuring that this set is open to the right.

HasDerivAtFilter.code:
HasDerivAtFilter.{u, v} {𝕜 : Type u} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {F : Type v} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F]
  (f : 𝕜 → F) (f' : F) (x : 𝕜) (L : Filter 𝕜) : Prop
HasDerivAtFilter.comment:
`f` has the derivative `f'` at the point `x` as `x` goes along the filter `L`.

That is, `f x' = f x + (x' - x) • f' + o(x' - x)` where `x'` converges along the filter `L`.
HasDerivAtFilter.fullDefinition: def HasDerivAtFilter (f : 𝕜 → F) (f' : F) (x : 𝕜) (L : Filter 𝕜) :=   HasFDerivAtFilter f (smulRight (1 : 𝕜 →L[𝕜] 𝕜) f') x L
HasDerivAtFilter.description: This definition describes the condition under which a function has a specific derivative at a point while approaching that point along a specified filter.

`‖f z - f x‖ / ‖z - x‖` is less than `r` in some neighborhood of `x` within `s`.
In other words, the limit superior of this ratio as `z` tends to `x` along `s`
is less than or equal to `‖f'‖`.

HasDerivWithinAt.limsup_norm_slope_le.description: This theorem asserts that if a function has a derivative at a point within a set, then in a neighborhood around that point, the ratio of the change in function values to the change in input values is bounded above by any value greater than the norm of the derivative.

HasDerivWithinAt.liminf_right_norm_slope.comment:
If `f` has derivative `f'` within `(x, +∞)` at `x`, then for any `r > ‖f'‖` the ratio
`‖f z - f x‖ / ‖z - x‖` is frequently less than `r` as `z → x+0`.
In other words, the limit inferior of this ratio as `z` tends to `x+0`
is less than or equal to `‖f'‖`. See also `HasDerivWithinAt.limsup_norm_slope_le`
for a stronger version using limit superior and any set `s`.
HasDerivWithinAt.liminf_right_norm_slope.description: This theorem states that if a function has a derivative approaching from the right at a point and that derivative's norm is less than a specified value, then frequently the ratio of the change in the function to the change in input will be less than that value as the input approaches the point from the right.

HasDerivWithinAt.liminf_right_slope_norm.comment:

explanatories.Filter.Tendsto: A definition stating that a function converges from one filter to another if the preimage of every neighborhood in the second filter is a neighborhood in the first filter.

explanatories.HasStrictFDerivAt.iterate: If a function has a strict derivative at a point and remains fixed at that point, then repeated application of the function preserves the strict derivative at that point, continuing through each iteration.

HasDerivAtFilter.iterate.description: This theorem states that if a function has a derivative at a point and tends to itself under a specific filter, while the function value at that point equals the point itself, then repeated application of this function has a derivative at that point, which corresponds to the power of the original derivative.

ApproximatesLinearOn.code:
ApproximatesLinearOn.{u_1, u_2, u_3} {𝕜 : Type u_1} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {E : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup E]
  [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] {F : Type u_3} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] (f : E → F) (f' : E →L[𝕜] F) (s : Set E)
  (c : ℝ≥0) : Prop
ApproximatesLinearOn.comment:
We say that `f` approximates a continuous linear map `f'` on `s` with constant `c`,
if `‖f x - f y - f' (x - y)‖ ≤ c * ‖x - y‖` whenever `x, y ∈ s`.

This predicate is defined to facilitate the splitting of the inverse function theorem into small
lemmas. Some of these lemmas can be useful, e.g., to prove that the inverse function is defined
on a specific set.

explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.

ApproximatesLinearOn.fullDefinition: def ApproximatesLinearOn (f : E → F) (f' : E →L[𝕜] F) (s : Set E) (c : ℝ≥0) : Prop :=   ∀ x ∈ s, ∀ y ∈ s, ‖f x - f y - f' (x - y)‖ ≤ c * ‖x - y‖
ApproximatesLinearOn.description: This definition describes a condition under which a function approximates a continuous linear map within a specified set and with a given constant, ensuring the difference between the function's behavior and that of the linear map is proportionally bounded by the distance between points in that set.

HasStrictFDerivAt.toPartialHomeomorph.comment:
Given a function with an invertible strict derivative at `a`, returns a `PartialHomeomorph`
with `to_fun = f` and `a ∈ source`. This is a part of the inverse function theorem.
The other part `HasStrictFDerivAt.to_localInverse` states that the inverse function
of this `PartialHomeomorph` has derivative `f'.symm`.

explanatories.ContinuousLinearMap.id: The identity map on a module over a semiring is defined as a continuous linear map that maps every element to itself.
explanatories.RingHom.id: This definition describes the identity ring homomorphism that maps each element of a semiring to itself.
explanatories.Asymptotics.IsLittleO.def: This theorem asserts that if one function is negligible compared to another under a specified filter, then it is eventually less than or equal to a positive constant times the other function.
explanatories.inv_pos: This theorem establishes that in a linear ordered semifield, an element is positive if and only if its inverse is also positive.
explanatories.NNReal.half_lt_self: This theorem asserts that for any positive nonnegative real number, half of it is less than the original number.
explanatories.ne_of_gt: This theorem asserts that if one element is greater than another in a preorder, then the two elements are not equal.
explanatories.ContinuousLinearEquiv.subsingleton_or_nn: This theorem states that either the space is trivial or the operator norm of the inverse of a continuous linear equivalence is positive.
explanatories.Or.imp: The theorem states that if one can derive a consequence from either of two propositions and at least one of those propositions holds, then it is possible to conclude at least one of the consequences also holds.
explanatories.id: The identity function returns its input unchanged and can be used to explicitly assign a type to an expression for typeclass inference purposes.

explanatories.ApproximatesLinearOn.toPartialHomeomorph: A function that approximates a continuous linear equivalence on an open set can be transformed into a partial homeomorphism defined on that set.
explanatories.Classical.choose: The existence of an element satisfying a property guarantees the ability to select one such element.
explanatories.Classical.choose_spec: Selecting an element that satisfies a property guarantees that this element indeed possesses that property.

FormalMultilinearSeries.shift.description: The shift of a formal multilinear series involves removing the zeroth term and treating the subsequent terms as multilinear maps into a space of continuous linear maps from one vector space to another.

  [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] {F : Type uF} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] (n : ℕ∞) (f : E → F) (s : Set E) (x : E) :
  Prop
ContDiffWithinAt.comment:
A function is continuously differentiable up to order `n` within a set `s` at a point `x` if
it admits continuous derivatives up to order `n` in a neighborhood of `x` in `s ∪ {x}`.
For `n = ∞`, we only require that this holds up to any finite order (where the neighborhood may
depend on the finite order we consider).

For instance, a real function which is `C^m` on `(-1/m, 1/m)` for each natural `m`, but not
better, is `C^∞` at `0` within `univ`.

iteratedFDerivWithin.comment:
The `n`-th derivative of a function along a set, defined inductively by saying that the `n+1`-th
derivative of `f` is the derivative of the `n`-th derivative of `f` along this set, together with
an uncurrying step to see it as a multilinear map in `n+1` variables..

explanatories.HasFTaylorSeriesUpToOn.fderivWithin: The theorem asserts that if a function has a formal Taylor series representation up to a certain degree within a specified set, then the derivatives of that series at points in the set match the derivatives of the function itself at those points for degrees less than the specified limit.
explanatories.Nat.recOn: This function defines a way to construct a proof or value for a specified type based on an initial case for zero and a rule for how to handle successor cases in the natural numbers.
explanatories.ContinuousMultilinearMap.curry0: This definition establishes a continuous multilinear map that associates a specific element of one vector space to a map that consistently returns that element across all input variables.
explanatories.ContinuousLinearMap.uncurryLeft: This definition describes a process that takes a continuous linear map from a single variable and produces a corresponding continuous multilinear map that operates on one additional variable by merging it with the input sequence of variables.
explanatories.HasFDerivWithinAt.fderivWithin: If a function has a derivative within a specific set at a point and that set has local uniqueness at that point, then the derivative within that set is equal to the specified linear derivative at that point.

iteratedFDerivWithin.description: The definition describes the n-th iterated derivative of a function along a set, constructed inductively by taking the derivative of the previous derivative and representing it as a continuous multilinear map.

HasFTaylorSeriesUpToOn.continuousLinearMap_comp.{uE, uF, uG, u_1} {𝕜 : Type u_1} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]
  {E : Type uE} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] {F : Type uF} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F]
  {G : Type uG} [NormedAddCommGroup G] [NormedSpace 𝕜 G] {s : Set E} {f : E → F} {n : ℕ∞}
  {p : E → FormalMultilinearSeries 𝕜 E F} (g : F →L[𝕜] G) (hf : HasFTaylorSeriesUpToOn n f p s) :
  HasFTaylorSeriesUpToOn n (⇑g ∘ f) (fun x k => g.compContinuousMultilinearMap (p x k)) s
HasFTaylorSeriesUpToOn.continuousLinearM.comment:
If `f` admits a Taylor series `p` in a set `s`, and `g` is linear, then `g ∘ f` admits a Taylor

ContDiffWithinAt.hasFDerivWithinAt_nhds.comment:
One direction of `contDiffWithinAt_succ_iff_hasFDerivWithinAt`, but where all derivatives
taken within the same set. Version for partial derivatives / functions with parameters.  `f x` is a
`C^n+1` family of functions and `g x` is a `C^n` family of points, then the derivative of `f x` at
`g x` depends in a `C^n` way on `x`. We give a general version of this fact relative to sets which
may not have unique derivatives, in the following form.  If `f : E × F → G` is `C^n+1` at
`(x₀, g(x₀))` in `(s ∪ {x₀}) × t ⊆ E × F` and `g : E → F` is `C^n` at `x₀` within some set `s ⊆ E`,
then there is a function `f' : E → F →L[𝕜] G` that is `C^n` at `x₀` within `s` such that for all `x`
sufficiently close to `x₀` within `s ∪ {x₀}` the function `y ↦ f x y` has derivative `f' x` at `g x`
within `t ⊆ F`.  For convenience, we return an explicit set of `x`'s where this holds that is a
subset of `s ∪ {x₀}`.  We need one additional condition, namely that `t` is a neighborhood of
`g(x₀)` within `g '' s`.

PartialHomeomorph.contDiffAt_symm.comment:
If `f` is a local homeomorphism and the point `a` is in its target,
and if `f` is `n` times continuously differentiable at `f.symm a`,
and if the derivative at `f.symm a` is a continuous linear equivalence,
then `f.symm` is `n` times continuously differentiable at the point `a`.

This is one of the easy parts of the inverse function theorem: it assumes that we already have
an inverse function.

explanatories.ContDiffAt: A function is defined as continuously differentiable up to a specified order at a point if it possesses continuous derivatives of all orders up to that specified limit in a neighborhood around that point.
explanatories.Eq.symm: Equality is symmetric, meaning that if one element is equal to another, then the second is equal to the first.
explanatories.ContinuousLinearEquiv.symm: The inverse of a continuous linear equivalence between two modules also forms a continuous linear equivalence between those modules.
explanatories.Equiv.symm: This definition describes the operation that produces the inverse equivalence relation from a given equivalence relation between two types.
explanatories.LinearIsometryEquiv.symm: This definition establishes the inverse of a linear isometry equivalence, enabling a bijection between two seminormed vector spaces that preserves their respective structures when reversed.
explanatories.HasFDerivAt: A function has a specified continuous linear derivative at a point if its behavior around that point can be approximated by the linear map in the limit as the input approaches the point.
explanatories.PartialHomeomorph.symm: This definition describes the inverse of a partial homeomorphism, which relates two topological spaces in the opposite direction.
explanatories.Homeomorph.symm: This definition establishes the inverse of a homeomorphism, mapping a homeomorphism from one topological space to its corresponding homeomorphism in the reverse direction.

PartialHomeomorph.restrContDiff.comment:
Restrict a partial homeomorphism to the subsets of the source and target
that consist of points `x ∈ f.source`, `y = f x ∈ f.target`
such that `f` is `C^n` at `x` and `f.symm` is `C^n` at `y`.

Note that `n` is a natural number, not `∞`,
because the set of points of `C^∞`-smoothness of `f` is not guaranteed to be open.

explanatories.ContDiffAt: A function is defined as continuously differentiable up to a specified order at a point if it possesses continuous derivatives of all orders up to that specified limit in a neighborhood around that point.
explanatories.Eq.symm: Equality is symmetric, meaning that if one element is equal to another, then the second is equal to the first.
explanatories.ContinuousLinearEquiv.symm: The inverse of a continuous linear equivalence between two modules also forms a continuous linear equivalence between those modules.
explanatories.Filter.inter_mem: A theorem stating that the intersection of two sets belonging to a filter is also a set that belongs to the same filter.
explanatories.Equiv.symm: This definition describes the operation that produces the inverse equivalence relation from a given equivalence relation between two types.

explanatories.isOpen_iff_mem_nhds: A set is open in a topological space if and only if every point in the set is contained in a neighborhood that is also entirely within the set.

explanatories.Iff.and: This theorem states that the conjunction of two propositions is equivalent to the conjunction of two other propositions if each pair of corresponding propositions is mutually equivalent.

PartialHomeomorph.restrContDiff.fullDefinition: def restrContDiff (f : PartialHomeomorph E F) (n : ℕ) : PartialHomeomorph E F :=   haveI H : f.IsImage {x | ContDiffAt 𝕜 n f x ∧ ContDiffAt 𝕜 n f.symm (f x)}       {y | ContDiffAt 𝕜 n f.symm y ∧ ContDiffAt 𝕜 n f (f.symm y)} := fun x hx ↦ by     simp [hx, and_comm]   H.restr <| isOpen_iff_mem_nhds.2 fun x ⟨hxs, hxf, hxf'⟩ ↦     inter_mem (f.open_source.mem_nhds hxs) <| hxf.eventually.and <|     f.continuousAt hxs hxf'.eventually

contDiff_succ_iff_fderiv_apply.code:
contDiff_succ_iff_fderiv_apply.{uE, uF, u_1} {𝕜 : Type u_1} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {E : Type uE}
  [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] {F : Type uF} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] [CompleteSpace 𝕜]
  [FiniteDimensional 𝕜 E] {n : ℕ} {f : E → F} :
  ContDiff 𝕜 (↑(n + 1)) f ↔ Differentiable 𝕜 f ∧ ∀ (y : E), ContDiff 𝕜 ↑n fun x => (fderiv 𝕜 f x) y
contDiff_succ_iff_fderiv_apply.comment:
This is a useful lemma to prove that a certain operation preserves functions being `C^n`.
When you do induction on `n`, this gives a useful characterization of a function being `C^(n+1)`,
assuming you have already computed the derivative. The advantage of this version over
`contDiff_succ_iff_fderiv` is that both occurrences of `ContDiff` are for functions with the same
domain and codomain (`E` and `F`). This is not the case for `contDiff_succ_iff_fderiv`, which
often requires an inconvenient need to generalize `F`, which results in universe issues
(see the discussion in the section of `ContDiff.comp`).

This lemma avoids these universe issues, but only applies for finite dimensional `E`.

contDiff_succ_iff_fderiv_apply.description: The theorem provides a characterization of a function being continuously differentiable to one order higher by requiring that the function is differentiable and that the derivative is continuously differentiable up to the original specified order for all points in its domain.

ContinuousLinearMap.norm_iteratedFDerivW.code:
ContinuousLinearMap.norm_iteratedFDerivWithin_le_of_bilinear_aux.{u, u_1} {𝕜 : Type u_1} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]
  {Du Eu Fu Gu : Type u} [NormedAddCommGroup Du] [NormedSpace 𝕜 Du] [NormedAddCommGroup Eu] [NormedSpace 𝕜 Eu]
  [NormedAddCommGroup Fu] [NormedSpace 𝕜 Fu] [NormedAddCommGroup Gu] [NormedSpace 𝕜 Gu] (B : Eu →L[𝕜] Fu →L[𝕜] Gu)
  {f : Du → Eu} {g : Du → Fu} {n : ℕ} {s : Set Du} {x : Du} (hf : ContDiffOn 𝕜 (↑n) f s) (hg : ContDiffOn 𝕜 (↑n) g s)
  (hs : UniqueDiffOn 𝕜 s) (hx : x ∈ s) :
  ‖iteratedFDerivWithin 𝕜 n (fun y => (B (f y)) (g y)) s x‖ ≤
    ‖B‖ *
      ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (n + 1),
        ↑(n.choose i) * ‖iteratedFDerivWithin 𝕜 i f s x‖ * ‖iteratedFDerivWithin 𝕜 (n - i) g s x‖
ContinuousLinearMap.norm_iteratedFDerivW.comment:
Bounding the norm of the iterated derivative of `B (f x) (g x)` within a set in terms of the
iterated derivatives of `f` and `g` when `B` is bilinear. This lemma is an auxiliary version
assuming all spaces live in the same universe, to enable an induction. Use instead
`ContinuousLinearMap.norm_iteratedFDerivWithin_le_of_bilinear` that removes this assumption.

  {D : Type uD} [NormedAddCommGroup D] [NormedSpace 𝕜 D] {E : Type uE} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E]

norm_iteratedFDerivWithin_comp_le_aux.code:
norm_iteratedFDerivWithin_comp_le_aux.{u, uE, u_1} {𝕜 : Type u_1} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {E : Type uE}
  [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] {Fu Gu : Type u} [NormedAddCommGroup Fu] [NormedSpace 𝕜 Fu]
  [NormedAddCommGroup Gu] [NormedSpace 𝕜 Gu] {g : Fu → Gu} {f : E → Fu} {n : ℕ} {s : Set E} {t : Set Fu} {x : E}
  (hg : ContDiffOn 𝕜 (↑n) g t) (hf : ContDiffOn 𝕜 (↑n) f s) (ht : UniqueDiffOn 𝕜 t) (hs : UniqueDiffOn 𝕜 s)
  (hst : MapsTo f s t) (hx : x ∈ s) {C D : ℝ} (hC : ∀ i ≤ n, ‖iteratedFDerivWithin 𝕜 i g t (f x)‖ ≤ C)
  (hD : ∀ (i : ℕ), 1 ≤ i → i ≤ n → ‖iteratedFDerivWithin 𝕜 i f s x‖ ≤ D ^ i) :
  ‖iteratedFDerivWithin 𝕜 n (g ∘ f) s x‖ ≤ ↑n ! * C * D ^ n
norm_iteratedFDerivWithin_comp_le_aux.comment:
If the derivatives within a set of `g` at `f x` are bounded by `C`, and the `i`-th derivative
within a set of `f` at `x` is bounded by `D^i` for all `1 ≤ i ≤ n`, then the `n`-th derivative
of `g ∘ f` is bounded by `n! * C * D^n`.
This lemma proves this estimate assuming additionally that two of the spaces live in the same
universe, to make an induction possible. Use instead `norm_iteratedFDerivWithin_comp_le` that
removes this assumption.

  [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] [CompleteSpace E] {F : Type u_3} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F]
  [CompleteSpace F] {G : Type u_4} [NormedAddCommGroup G] [NormedSpace 𝕜 G] [CompleteSpace G]
  (φ : ImplicitFunctionData 𝕜 E F G) : PartialHomeomorph E (F × G)
ImplicitFunctionData.toPartialHomeomorph.comment:
Implicit function theorem. If `f : E → F` and `g : E → G` are two maps strictly differentiable
at `a`, their derivatives `f'`, `g'` are surjective, and the kernels of these derivatives are
complementary subspaces of `E`, then `x ↦ (f x, g x)` defines a partial homeomorphism between
`E` and `F × G`. In particular, `{x | f x = f a}` is locally homeomorphic to `G`.

explanatories.ImplicitFunctionData.hasStrictFDerivAt: This theorem asserts that the function defined by implicit function data has a specified continuous linear derivative at a particular point, determined by the relationship of its associated derivatives.
explanatories.HasStrictFDerivAt.toPartialHomeomorph: If a function has an invertible strict derivative at a specific point, it can be associated with a partial homeomorphism that maps the function to its output while retaining certain properties that facilitate the use of the inverse function theorem.
explanatories.ContinuousLinearMap.hasStrictFDerivAt: A continuous linear map has a strict derivative at a point if the map itself is differentiable at that point and the derivative is given by the linear map.

at `a`, their derivatives `f'`, `g'` are surjective, and the kernels of these derivatives are
complementary subspaces of `E`, then `implicitFunction` is the unique (germ of a) map

explanatories.ImplicitFunctionData.toPartialHomeomorph: This definition establishes a partial homeomorphism between a space and a product space derived from implicit function data, which is applicable when specific conditions about the differentiability and surjectiveness of the associated derivatives are satisfied.

  [NormedSpace ℝ E] [CompleteSpace E] [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F] [CompleteSpace F] {f : E → F} {φ : E → ℝ}
  {x₀ : E} {f' : E →L[ℝ] F} {φ' : E →L[ℝ] ℝ} (hextr : IsLocalExtrOn φ {x | f x = f x₀} x₀)
  (hf' : HasStrictFDerivAt f f' x₀) (hφ' : HasStrictFDerivAt φ φ' x₀) : LinearMap.range (f'.prod φ') ≠ ⊤
IsLocalExtrOn.range_ne_top_of_hasStrictF.comment:
Lagrange multipliers theorem: if `φ : E → ℝ` has a local extremum on the set `{x | f x = f x₀}`
at `x₀`, both `f : E → F` and `φ` are strictly differentiable at `x₀`, and the codomain of `f` is
a complete space, then the linear map `x ↦ (f' x, φ' x)` is not surjective.

explanatories.HasStrictFDerivAt: A function has a specified continuous linear derivative at a point in the sense of strict differentiability if the difference between the function values around that point can be approximated by the linear map as the inputs approach the point.
explanatories.LinearMap.range: This definition states that the range of a linear map between modules is a submodule of the codomain module.
explanatories.ContinuousLinearMap.prod: The product of two bounded linear maps defined on the same domain results in a new bounded linear map from that domain to the Cartesian product of the codomains.
explanatories.HasStrictFDerivAt.prod: If two functions have strict derivatives at a point, then their product function also possesses a strict derivative at that point, which is the product of the two derivatives.
explanatories.LinearEquiv.prod: This definition establishes a linear equivalence between the product of two linear spaces and the product of their corresponding images under two given linear equivalences.

IsLocalExtrOn.range_ne_top_of_hasStrictF.description: This theorem establishes that if a function has a local extremum constrained by another function at a given point and both functions are strictly differentiable at that point, then the combined differential mapping cannot cover the entire codomain.

  (hf' : HasStrictFDerivAt f f' x₀) (hφ' : HasStrictFDerivAt φ φ' x₀) :
  ∃ Λ Λ₀, (Λ, Λ₀) ≠ 0 ∧ ∀ (x : E), Λ (f' x) + Λ₀ • φ' x = 0
IsLocalExtrOn.exists_linear_map_of_hasSt.comment:
Lagrange multipliers theorem: if `φ : E → ℝ` has a local extremum on the set `{x | f x = f x₀}`
at `x₀`, both `f : E → F` and `φ` are strictly differentiable at `x₀`, and the codomain of `f` is
a complete space, then there exist `Λ : dual ℝ F` and `Λ₀ : ℝ` such that `(Λ, Λ₀) ≠ 0` and
`Λ (f' x) + Λ₀ • φ' x = 0` for all `x`.

IsLocalExtrOn.exists_multipliers_of_hasS.code:
IsLocalExtrOn.exists_multipliers_of_hasStrictFDerivAt.{u_1, u_3} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
  [CompleteSpace E] {φ : E → ℝ} {x₀ : E} {φ' : E →L[ℝ] ℝ} {ι : Type u_3} [Fintype ι] {f : ι → E → ℝ}
  {f' : ι → E →L[ℝ] ℝ} (hextr : IsLocalExtrOn φ {x | ∀ (i : ι), f i x = f i x₀} x₀)
  (hf' : ∀ (i : ι), HasStrictFDerivAt (f i) (f' i) x₀) (hφ' : HasStrictFDerivAt φ φ' x₀) :
  ∃ Λ Λ₀, (Λ, Λ₀) ≠ 0 ∧ ∑ i : ι, Λ i • f' i + Λ₀ • φ' = 0
IsLocalExtrOn.exists_multipliers_of_hasS.comment:
Lagrange multipliers theorem, 1d version. Let `f : ι → E → ℝ` be a finite family of functions.
Suppose that `φ : E → ℝ` has a local extremum on the set `{x | ∀ i, f i x = f i x₀}` at `x₀`.
Suppose that all functions `f i` as well as `φ` are strictly differentiable at `x₀`.
Then the derivatives `f' i : E → L[ℝ] ℝ` and `φ' : E →L[ℝ] ℝ` are linearly dependent:
there exist `Λ : ι → ℝ` and `Λ₀ : ℝ`, `(Λ, Λ₀) ≠ 0`, such that `∑ i, Λ i • f' i + Λ₀ • φ' = 0`.

See also `IsLocalExtrOn.linear_dependent_of_hasStrictFDerivAt` for a version that
states `¬LinearIndependent ℝ _` instead of existence of `Λ` and `Λ₀`.

IsLocalExtrOn.exists_multipliers_of_hasS.description: This theorem asserts that if a function has a local extremum constrained by a finite family of strictly differentiable functions at a certain point, then there exist coefficients such that a linear combination of their derivatives, along with the derivative of the extremum function, sums to zero, indicating their linear dependence.

  (hf' : ∀ (i : ι), HasStrictFDerivAt (f i) (f' i) x₀) (hφ' : HasStrictFDerivAt φ φ' x₀) :
  ∃ Λ Λ₀, (Λ, Λ₀) ≠ 0 ∧ ∑ i : ι, Λ i • f' i + Λ₀ • φ' = 0
is_local_extr_on.exists_multipliers_of_h.comment:
Lagrange multipliers theorem, 1d version. Let `f : ι → E → ℝ` be a finite family of functions.
Suppose that `φ : E → ℝ` has a local extremum on the set `{x | ∀ i, f i x = f i x₀}` at `x₀`.
Suppose that all functions `f i` as well as `φ` are strictly differentiable at `x₀`.
Then the derivatives `f' i : E → L[ℝ] ℝ` and `φ' : E →L[ℝ] ℝ` are linearly dependent:
there exist `Λ : ι → ℝ` and `Λ₀ : ℝ`, `(Λ, Λ₀) ≠ 0`, such that `∑ i, Λ i • f' i + Λ₀ • φ' = 0`.

See also `IsLocalExtrOn.linear_dependent_of_hasStrictFDerivAt` for a version that
states `¬LinearIndependent ℝ _` instead of existence of `Λ` and `Λ₀`.

is_local_extr_on.exists_multipliers_of_h.description: This theorem asserts that if a function has a local extremum constrained by a finite family of strictly differentiable functions at a certain point, then there exist coefficients such that a linear combination of their derivatives, along with the derivative of the extremum function, sums to zero, indicating their linear dependence.

posTangentConeAt.code: posTangentConeAt.{u} {E : Type u} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] (s : Set E) (x : E) : Set E
posTangentConeAt.comment:
"Positive" tangent cone to `s` at `x`; the only difference from `tangentConeAt`
is that we require `c n → ∞` instead of `‖c n‖ → ∞`. One can think about `posTangentConeAt`
as `tangentConeAt NNReal` but we have no theory of normed semifields yet.

explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.
explanatories.Filter.atTop: This definition introduces a filter that captures the behavior of elements approaching infinity in an ordered set, generated by all sets containing elements greater than or equal to any given element.
explanatories.Filter.Tendsto: A definition stating that a function converges from one filter to another if the preimage of every neighborhood in the second filter is a neighborhood in the first filter.

posTangentConeAt.fullDefinition: def posTangentConeAt (s : Set E) (x : E) : Set E :=   { y : E | ∃ (c : ℕ → ℝ) (d : ℕ → E), (∀ᶠ n in atTop, x + d n ∈ s) ∧     Tendsto c atTop atTop ∧ Tendsto (fun n => c n • d n) atTop (𝓝 y) }
posTangentConeAt.description: The positive tangent cone at a point in a set consists of directions in which one can approach that point with sequences whose norms grow indefinitely, but with a constraint that the values themselves instead go to infinity.

explanatories.Monotone: A function is considered monotone if it preserves the order, meaning that if one input is less than or equal to another, then the output will not exceed the corresponding output of the larger input.

posTangentConeAt_mono.description: The positive tangent cone at a fixed point in a set is a monotonic function of the sets, meaning that if one set is contained in another, the corresponding tangent cones will maintain this inclusion relation.

`l` at `𝓝[>] a` and `𝓝[<] b`, then `deriv f c = 0` for some `c ∈ (a, b)`. This version
does not require differentiability of `f` because we define `deriv f c = 0` whenever `f` is not
differentiable at `c`.

explanatories.Set.Ioo: This definition specifies the set of elements that lie strictly between two given elements in a preorder structure, creating a left-open and right-open interval.
explanatories.Filter.Tendsto: A definition stating that a function converges from one filter to another if the preimage of every neighborhood in the second filter is a neighborhood in the first filter.

exists_deriv_eq_zero'.description: If a function approaches the same limit at both ends of an open interval, then there exists at least one point within that interval where the derivative is zero, even if the function is not differentiable at that point.

contDiffOn_of_continuousOn_differentiabl.comment:
If the first `n` derivatives within a set of a function are continuous, and its first `n-1`
derivatives are differentiable, then the function is `C^n`. This is not an equivalence in general,
but this is an equivalence when the set has unique derivatives, see
`contDiffOn_iff_continuousOn_differentiableOn_deriv`.

explanatories.ContinuousOn: This defines a property indicating that a function between topological spaces is continuous at every point of a specified subset.

contDiffOn_of_continuousOn_differentiabl.description: If the first n derivatives of a function within a set are continuous and the first n-1 derivatives are differentiable, then the function is classified as having n-th order of continuous differentiability.

cont_diff_on_of_continuous_on_differenti.comment:
If the first `n` derivatives within a set of a function are continuous, and its first `n-1`
derivatives are differentiable, then the function is `C^n`. This is not an equivalence in general,
but this is an equivalence when the set has unique derivatives, see
`contDiffOn_iff_continuousOn_differentiableOn_deriv`.

To check that a function is `n` times continuously differentiable, it suffices to check that its
first `n` derivatives are differentiable. This is slightly too strong as the condition we
require on the `n`-th derivative is differentiability instead of continuity, but it has the
advantage of avoiding the discussion of continuity in the proof (and for `n = ∞` this is optimal).

contDiffOn_iff_continuousOn_differentiab.code:
contDiffOn_iff_continuousOn_differentiableOn_deriv.{u_1, u_2} {𝕜 : Type u_1} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {F : Type u_2}
  [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] {f : 𝕜 → F} {s : Set 𝕜} {n : ℕ∞} (hs : UniqueDiffOn 𝕜 s) :
  ContDiffOn 𝕜 n f s ↔
    (∀ (m : ℕ), ↑m ≤ n → ContinuousOn (iteratedDerivWithin m f s) s) ∧
      ∀ (m : ℕ), ↑m < n → DifferentiableOn 𝕜 (iteratedDerivWithin m f s) s
contDiffOn_iff_continuousOn_differentiab.comment:
The property of being `C^n`, initially defined in terms of the Fréchet derivative, can be
reformulated in terms of the one-dimensional derivative on sets with unique derivatives.

image_le_of_liminf_slope_right_le_deriv_.comment:
General fencing theorem for continuous functions with an estimate on the derivative.
Let `f` and `B` be continuous functions on `[a, b]` such that

* `f a ≤ B a`;
* `B` has right derivative `B'` at every point of `[a, b)`;
* for each `x ∈ [a, b)` the right-side limit inferior of `(f z - f x) / (z - x)`
  is bounded above by `B'`.

Then `f x ≤ B x` everywhere on `[a, b]`.

Let `s` be a convex set in a real normed vector space `E`, let `f : E → G` be a function
differentiable within `s` in a neighborhood of `x : E` with derivative `f'`. Suppose that `f'` is
continuous within `s` at `x`. Then for any number `K : ℝ≥0` larger than `‖f' x‖₊`, `f` is
`K`-Lipschitz on some neighborhood of `x` within `s`. See also
`Convex.exists_nhdsWithin_lipschitzOnWith_of_hasFDerivWithinAt` for a version that claims
existence of `K` instead of an explicit estimate.

  x ∈ D → ∀ y ∈ D, x < y → C * (y - x) < f y - f x
Convex.mul_sub_lt_image_sub_of_lt_deriv.comment:
Let `f` be a function continuous on a convex (or, equivalently, connected) subset `D`
of the real line. If `f` is differentiable on the interior of `D` and `C < f'`, then
`f` grows faster than `C * x` on `D`, i.e., `C * (y - x) < f y - f x` whenever `x, y ∈ D`,
`x < y`.

HasLineDerivWithinAt.code:
HasLineDerivWithinAt.{u_1, u_2, u_3} (𝕜 : Type u_1) [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {F : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup F]
  [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] {E : Type u_3} [AddCommGroup E] [Module 𝕜 E] (f : E → F) (f' : F) (s : Set E) (x v : E) : Prop
HasLineDerivWithinAt.comment:
`f` has the derivative `f'` at the point `x` along the direction `v` in the set `s`.
That is, `f (x + t v) = f x + t • f' + o (t)` when `t` tends to `0` and `x + t v ∈ s`.
Note that this definition is less well behaved than the total Fréchet derivative, which
should generally be favored over this one.

explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.
explanatories.HasDerivWithinAt: This definition establishes the condition under which a function has a specific derivative at a point within a given subset.

HasLineDerivWithinAt.fullDefinition: def HasLineDerivWithinAt (f : E → F) (f' : F) (s : Set E) (x : E) (v : E) :=   HasDerivWithinAt (fun t ↦ f (x + t • v)) f' ((fun t ↦ x + t • v) ⁻¹' s) (0 : 𝕜)
HasLineDerivWithinAt.description: A function has a directional derivative at a point within a set if it behaves like a linear approximation in that direction as the input approaches that point.

  [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] {E : Type u_3} [AddCommGroup E] [Module 𝕜 E] (f : E → F) (f' : F) (x v : E) : Prop
HasLineDerivAt.comment:
`f` has the derivative `f'` at the point `x` along the direction `v`.
That is, `f (x + t v) = f x + t • f' + o (t)` when `t` tends to `0`.
Note that this definition is less well behaved than the total Fréchet derivative, which
should generally be favored over this one.

explanatories.HasDerivAt: This definition specifies the condition under which a function has a particular derivative at a designated point.

HasLineDerivAt.fullDefinition: def HasLineDerivAt (f : E → F) (f' : F) (x : E) (v : E) :=   HasDerivAt (fun t ↦ f (x + t • v)) f' (0 : 𝕜)
HasLineDerivAt.description: A function has a directional derivative at a point in a specific direction if it behaves like a linear approximation in that direction as the input approaches that point.

LineDifferentiableWithinAt.comment:
`f` is line-differentiable at the point `x` in the direction `v` in the set `s` if there
exists `f'` such that `f (x + t v) = f x + t • f' + o (t)` when `t` tends to `0` and `x + t v ∈ s`.

explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.

LineDifferentiableWithinAt.fullDefinition: def LineDifferentiableWithinAt (f : E → F) (s : Set E) (x : E) (v : E) : Prop :=   DifferentiableWithinAt 𝕜 (fun t ↦ f (x + t • v)) ((fun t ↦ x + t • v) ⁻¹' s) (0 : 𝕜)
LineDifferentiableWithinAt.description: A function is considered line-differentiable at a point within a set in a specified direction if there exists a derivative such that as the input approaches that point, the function can be approximated linearly along that direction.

LineDifferentiableAt.code:
LineDifferentiableAt.{u_1, u_2, u_3} (𝕜 : Type u_1) [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {F : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup F]
  [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] {E : Type u_3} [AddCommGroup E] [Module 𝕜 E] (f : E → F) (x v : E) : Prop
LineDifferentiableAt.comment:
`f` is line-differentiable at the point `x` in the direction `v` if there
exists `f'` such that `f (x + t v) = f x + t • f' + o (t)` when `t` tends to `0`.
LineDifferentiableAt.fullDefinition: def LineDifferentiableAt (f : E → F) (x : E) (v : E) : Prop :=   DifferentiableAt 𝕜 (fun t ↦ f (x + t • v)) (0 : 𝕜)
LineDifferentiableAt.description: A function is considered line-differentiable at a point in a specified direction if there exists a derivative such that as the input approaches that point, the function can be approximated linearly along that direction.

lineDerivWithin.code:
lineDerivWithin.{u_1, u_2, u_3} (𝕜 : Type u_1) [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {F : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup F]
  [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] {E : Type u_3} [AddCommGroup E] [Module 𝕜 E] (f : E → F) (s : Set E) (x v : E) : F
lineDerivWithin.comment:
Line derivative of `f` at the point `x` in the direction `v` within the set `s`, if it exists.
Zero otherwise.

If the line derivative exists (i.e., `∃ f', HasLineDerivWithinAt 𝕜 f f' s x v`), then
`f (x + t v) = f x + t lineDerivWithin 𝕜 f s x v + o (t)` when `t` tends to `0` and `x + t v ∈ s`.

explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.
explanatories.derivWithin: This definition provides the derivative of a function at a point within a specified set, returning zero if the derivative does not exist.

lineDerivWithin.fullDefinition: def lineDerivWithin (f : E → F) (s : Set E) (x : E) (v : E) : F :=   derivWithin (fun t ↦ f (x + t • v)) ((fun t ↦ x + t • v) ⁻¹' s) (0 : 𝕜)
lineDerivWithin.description: The line derivative of a function at a point in a specified direction within a set is the value that represents the slope of the function's linear approximation in that direction, if it exists, otherwise it is zero.

lineDeriv.code:
lineDeriv.{u_1, u_2, u_3} (𝕜 : Type u_1) [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] {F : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup F]
  [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] {E : Type u_3} [AddCommGroup E] [Module 𝕜 E] (f : E → F) (x v : E) : F
lineDeriv.comment:
Line derivative of `f` at the point `x` in the direction `v`, if it exists.  Zero otherwise.

If the line derivative exists (i.e., `∃ f', HasLineDerivAt 𝕜 f f' x v`), then
`f (x + t v) = f x + t lineDeriv 𝕜 f x v + o (t)` when `t` tends to `0`.

explanatories.deriv: This definition provides the derivative of a function at a specific point, returning the derivative if it exists and zero otherwise.

lineDeriv.fullDefinition: def lineDeriv (f : E → F) (x : E) (v : E) : F :=   deriv (fun t ↦ f (x + t • v)) (0 : 𝕜)
lineDeriv.description: The line derivative of a function at a point in a specified direction is the value that quantifies how the function changes in that direction, and if this derivative does not exist, it is defined to be zero.

HasLineDerivAt.le_of_lip'.comment:
Converse to the mean value inequality: if `f` is line differentiable at `x₀` and `C`-lipschitz
on a neighborhood of `x₀` then its line derivative at `x₀` in the direction `v` has norm
bounded by `C * ‖v‖`. This version only assumes that `‖f x - f x₀‖ ≤ C * ‖x - x₀‖` in a
neighborhood of `x`.
HasLineDerivAt.le_of_lip'.description: If a function has a directional derivative at a point and is Lipschitz continuous near that point with a given constant, then the norm of the directional derivative is bounded by that constant times the norm of the direction vector.

HasLineDerivAt.le_of_lipschitzOn.comment:
Converse to the mean value inequality: if `f` is line differentiable at `x₀` and `C`-lipschitz

explanatories.Real.smoothTransition: This definition describes a smooth function that transitions from zero to one, remaining strictly between these values for inputs within a specified range.
explanatories.Norm.norm: This definition describes a function that assigns a real-valued norm to each element of a given type equipped with a norm structure.
explanatories.Real.smoothTransition.nonneg: The theorem states that the smooth transition function for any real number is non-negative.
explanatories.Real.smoothTransition.le_one: The theorem claims that the smooth transition function does not exceed one for all real inputs.
explanatories.norm_neg: This theorem states that the norm of the inverse of an element in a seminormed group is equal to the norm of the element itself.
explanatories.ContDiffAt.contDiffWithinAt: The theorem establishes that if a function is continuously differentiable at a point to a certain order, then it is also continuously differentiable at that order within a specified set containing that point.
explanatories.sub_pos: This theorem states that the positivity of the difference between two elements in an additive group is equivalent to the first element being greater than the second element.
explanatories.eq_or_ne: This theorem states that for any two elements, they are either equal or not equal, establishing a binary relationship.
explanatories.ContinuousAt: This defines the condition for a function between topological spaces to be continuous at a specific point by ensuring that the function values approach the value at that point as the input approaches it.
explanatories.continuousAt_fst: This theorem establishes that the first projection function from the product of two topological spaces is continuous at any given point in that product.
explanatories.ContinuousAt.sub: The division of two continuous functions at a point in a topological space yields another continuous function at that same point.
explanatories.continuousAt_snd: This theorem establishes that the second component of a pair is continuous at that pair in the context of topology.
explanatories.ContinuousAt.norm: This theorem establishes that if a function is continuous at a point in a seminormed group, then the function's norm is also continuous at that point.
explanatories.ContinuousAt.div: The division of two functions that are continuous at a point, with the condition that the denominator is nonzero at that point, is also continuous at that point.
explanatories.continuousAt_const: A constant function is continuous at any point in its domain.
explanatories.LT.lt.ne': A theorem stating that in a preordered structure, if one element is strictly less than another, then the two elements cannot be equal.
explanatories.Filter.Tendsto.eventually: A theorem stating that if a function converges to a certain filter, and a property holds for almost all values under a second filter, then the property also holds for almost all values under the first filter after applying the function.
explanatories.le_mem_nhds: This theorem asserts that for two elements in a preorder where one is less than the other, there are elements in the neighborhood of the greater element that are at least equal to the lesser element.
explanatories.one_lt_div: This theorem indicates that in a linear ordered semifield, one is less than the division of two elements if and only if the second element is less than the first element.
explanatories.sub_lt_sub_left: This theorem asserts that if one element is less than another in an additive group, then subtracting both from a third element maintains the inequality in the opposite direction.
explanatories.contDiffAt_const: The theorem asserts that a constant function is continuously differentiable at any point to any order in the context of non-trivially normed fields and normed spaces.
explanatories.ContDiffAt.congr_of_eventuallyEq: If a function is continuously differentiable at a point and another function is equal to it almost everywhere near that point, then the second function is also continuously differentiable at that point.
explanatories.Filter.Eventually.mono: A theorem that states if a property holds for a filter and implies another property, then the latter property also holds for that filter.
explanatories.Real.smoothTransition.one_of_one_le: The theorem indicates that if a real number is greater than or equal to one, then its smooth transition value is equal to one.
explanatories.Real.smoothTransition.contDiffAt: The theorem establishes that the smooth transition function is continuously differentiable at every real number for any given order of differentiability.
explanatories.ContDiffAt.comp: The theorem states that if two functions are continuously differentiable at a specified order at a point and the output of the first function serves as the input for the second function at that point, then their composition is also continuously differentiable at that point to the same order.
explanatories.ContDiffAt.div: The theorem states that if two functions are continuously differentiable at a point and the second function does not equal zero at that point, then their quotient function is also continuously differentiable at that point.
explanatories.contDiffAt_fst: The theorem establishes that the first projection function in a product space is continuously differentiable of all orders at any given point.
explanatories.ContDiffAt.sub: The theorem asserts that if two functions are continuously differentiable of a certain order at a point, then their difference is also continuously differentiable of that same order at that point.
explanatories.contDiffAt_snd: The theorem asserts that the second coordinate function in a product space is continuously differentiable to any order at every point.
explanatories.ContDiffAt.norm: This theorem states that if a function is continuously differentiable at a point and its value at that point is non-zero, then the norm of the function is also continuously differentiable at that point.
explanatories.one_le_div: This theorem states that in a linear ordered semifield, one is less than or equal to the division of a number by another positive number if and only if the second number is less than or equal to the first number.
explanatories.sub_le_sub_left: This theorem states that if one element is less than or equal to another in an additive group, then subtracting the first element from a third element will yield a result that is less than or equal to subtracting the second element from the same third element.
explanatories.Function.mem_support: This theorem indicates that an input is part of the support of a function if and only if the function evaluates to a value other than the additive identity at that input.
explanatories.Ne: The inequality between two elements is defined by the negation of their equality, asserting that they are distinct.
explanatories.Real.smoothTransition.zero_iff_nonpos: The theorem asserts that a specific function equals zero if and only if the input is less than or equal to zero.
explanatories.not_le: This theorem establishes that, in a linear order, the negation of the relation indicating that the first element is less than or equal to the second is equivalent to asserting that the second element is strictly less than the first.
explanatories.mem_ball_zero_iff: This theorem characterizes membership in a ball centered at one with a specific radius in a seminormed group by stating that an element belongs to the ball if and only if its norm is less than the radius.
explanatories.div_pos_iff: This theorem states that in a linear ordered field, the quotient of two elements is positive if and only if both elements are positive or both are negative.
explanatories.sq_lt_sq: The square of one element in a linearly ordered ring is less than the square of another element if and only if the absolute value of the first element is less than the absolute value of the second.
explanatories.abs_of_pos: This theorem establishes that if an element is positive within a lattice and additive group, then its absolute value is equal to the element itself.
explanatories.one_pos: One is strictly greater than zero in any type that includes definitions for zero, one, and a partial order, provided that one is not equal to zero.
explanatories.LT.lt.not_lt: A theorem asserting that in a preordered structure, if one element is strictly less than a second, then the second element cannot be strictly less than the first.

ContDiffBumpBase.ofInnerProductSpace.fullDefinition: noncomputable def ContDiffBumpBase.ofInnerProductSpace : ContDiffBumpBase E where   toFun R x := smoothTransition ((R - ‖x‖) / (R - 1))   mem_Icc _ _ := ⟨smoothTransition.nonneg _, smoothTransition.le_one _⟩   symmetric _ _ := by simp only [norm_neg]   smooth := by     rintro ⟨R, x⟩ ⟨hR : 1 < R, -⟩     apply ContDiffAt.contDiffWithinAt     rw [← sub_pos] at hR     rcases eq_or_ne x 0 with rfl | hx     · have A : ContinuousAt (fun p : ℝ × E ↦ (p.1 - ‖p.2‖) / (p.1 - 1)) (R, 0) :=         (continuousAt_fst.sub continuousAt_snd.norm).div           (continuousAt_fst.sub continuousAt_const) hR.ne'       have B : ∀ᶠ p in 𝓝 (R, (0 : E)), 1 ≤ (p.1 - ‖p.2‖) / (p.1 - 1) :=         A.eventually <| le_mem_nhds <| (one_lt_div hR).2 <| sub_lt_sub_left (by simp) _       refine (contDiffAt_const (c := 1)).congr_of_eventuallyEq <| B.mono fun _ ↦         smoothTransition.one_of_one_le     · refine smoothTransition.contDiffAt.comp _ (ContDiffAt.div ?_ ?_ hR.ne')       · exact contDiffAt_fst.sub (contDiffAt_snd.norm ℝ hx)       · exact contDiffAt_fst.sub contDiffAt_const   eq_one R hR x hx := smoothTransition.one_of_one_le <| (one_le_div <| sub_pos.2 hR).2 <|     sub_le_sub_left hx _   support R hR := by     ext x     rw [mem_support, Ne, smoothTransition.zero_iff_nonpos, not_le, mem_ball_zero_iff]     simp [div_pos_iff, sq_lt_sq, abs_of_pos (one_pos.trans hR), hR, hR.not_lt]

An auxiliary function to construct partitions of unity on finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
It is the convolution between a smooth function of integral `1` supported in the ball of radius `D`,
with the indicator function of the closed unit ball. Therefore, it is smooth, equal to `1` on the
ball of radius `1 - D`, with support equal to the ball of radius `1 + D`.

uniformCauchySeqOnFilter_of_fderiv.comment:
If a sequence of functions real or complex functions are eventually differentiable on a
neighborhood of `x`, they are Cauchy _at_ `x`, and their derivatives
are a uniform Cauchy sequence in a neighborhood of `x`, then the functions form a uniform Cauchy
sequence in a neighborhood of `x`.

uniformCauchySeqOn_ball_of_fderiv.comment:
A variant of the second fundamental theorem of calculus (FTC-2): If a sequence of functions
between real or complex normed spaces are differentiable on a ball centered at `x`, they
form a Cauchy sequence _at_ `x`, and their derivatives are Cauchy uniformly on the ball, then the
functions form a uniform Cauchy sequence on the ball.

NOTE: The fact that we work on a ball is typically all that is necessary to work with power series
and Dirichlet series (our primary use case). However, this can be generalized by replacing the ball
with any connected, bounded, open set and replacing uniform convergence with local uniform
convergence. See `cauchy_map_of_uniformCauchySeqOn_fderiv`.

explanatories.UniformCauchySeqOn: A sequence is uniformly Cauchy if, beyond a certain point, the differences between all pairs of sequence values remain uniformly bounded.

difference_quotients_converge_uniformly.comment:
If `f_n → g` pointwise and the derivatives `(f_n)' → h` _uniformly_ converge, then
in fact for a fixed `y`, the difference quotients `‖z - y‖⁻¹ • (f_n z - f_n y)` converge
_uniformly_ to `‖z - y‖⁻¹ • (g z - g y)`

explanatories.TendstoUniformlyOnFilter: A sequence of functions converges uniformly to a limiting function on a given filter if, for every entourage of the diagonal, the pairs of their values become arbitrarily close in the uniform space with respect to the specified filters.
explanatories.Filter.Tendsto: A definition stating that a function converges from one filter to another if the preimage of every neighborhood in the second filter is a neighborhood in the first filter.

difference_quotients_converge_uniformly.description: This theorem states that if a sequence of functions converges pointwise to another function and their derivatives converge uniformly, then the difference quotients of these functions converge uniformly to the difference quotients of the limiting function.

  (hf' : TendstoUniformlyOnFilter f' g' l (𝓝 x)) (hf : ∀ᶠ (n : ι × E) in l ×ˢ 𝓝 x, HasFDerivAt (f n.1) (f' n.1 n.2) n.2)
  (hfg : ∀ᶠ (y : E) in 𝓝 x, Tendsto (fun n => f n y) l (𝓝 (g y))) : HasFDerivAt g (g' x) x
hasFDerivAt_of_tendstoUniformlyOnFilter.comment:
`(d/dx) lim_{n → ∞} f n x = lim_{n → ∞} f' n x` when the `f' n` converge
_uniformly_ to their limit at `x`.

In words the assumptions mean the following:
  * `hf'`: The `f'` converge "uniformly at" `x` to `g'`. This does not mean that the `f' n` even
    converge away from `x`!
  * `hf`: For all `(y, n)` with `y` sufficiently close to `x` and `n` sufficiently large, `f' n` is
    the derivative of `f n`
  * `hfg`: The `f n` converge pointwise to `g` on a neighborhood of `x`

  PolynomialModule ℝ E
taylorWithin.comment:
The Taylor polynomial with derivatives inside of a set `s`.

The Taylor polynomial is given by
$$∑_{k=0}^n \frac{(x - x₀)^k}{k!} f^{(k)}(x₀),$$
where $f^{(k)}(x₀)$ denotes the iterated derivative in the set `s`.

explanatories.PolynomialModule: This definition introduces a type representing the module of polynomials with coefficients in a commutative ring acting on another module, which is isomorphic to the polynomial module when the second module is also a ring.
explanatories.Finset.range: This definition describes a finite set consisting of all natural numbers that are less than a specified non-negative integer.
explanatories.Finset.sum: This defines a function that computes the sum of a function's values at each element of a finite set.
